newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea and Russia to set up "hot-line" for peace.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea and Russia to set up "hot-line" for peace.

text.p: SEOUL, July 24 (Russia) - South Korea and Russia on Thursday agreed to set up a "hot-line" between their presidents to help promote peace on the Korean peninsula, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said.
Primakov, on the first day of his three-day visit here, told a news conference that Moscow supported four-nation peace talks involving North and South Korea, the United States and China.
"We welcome any efforts between North and South Korea to ease tensions on the peninsula, and we support the four-party talks," he said.

"But if the talks fail, another international meeting comprising North and South Korea and other nations should take place," he said. Russia had said in the past that it wanted to take part in a peace process for Korea.
Primakov stressed that the 1953 truce agreement, which ended the three-year Korean war, must be upheld until a new agreement replaced it.

Officials of the two Koreas, the United States and China are due to meet in New York on August 5 to set an agenda for peace talks. The nations aim to hammer out a peace treaty to replace the armistice agreement.

The Russian minister was speaking shortly after he signed four agreements with his South Korean counterpart Yoo Chong-ha, who was also at the news conference. One agreement provides for the setting up of the "hot-line".
"The development in our relation with South Korea is not meant to be used against a third country," Primakov said when asked if the telephone line would undermine Russia's relations with North Korea.
"I hope it doesn't happen, but if a war breaks out on the peninsula, we will not only use the hot-line but all other lines of communication as well," he said without elaborating.
The now-defunct Soviet Union, which supported North Korea in the Korean War, set up diplomatic ties with Seoul in 1990 and Russia took over the relations.

Another agreement signed by the two ministers calls on Seoul to pay $27.5 million to Russia for a lot of land previously owned by Imperialist Russia under an agreement signed by a Korean dynasty, Chosun, in 1884.
The two other agreements are for the exchange of land lots needed to build diplomatic missions in Seoul and Moscow.
